table.text: The discovery (n=55,839) and replication (n=23,932) datasets included participants recruited from assessment centers in England using a 70/30 random split stratified by age, sex and number of valid dietary recalls.
The validation dataset (n=7,391) included all participants recruited from Scotland and Wales, providing an independent test of generalizability across regional dietary cultures.

First occurrences data were accessed on 22 September 2022, with censoring dates of 30 September 2021, 31 July 2021, and 31 October 2021 for participants recruited in England, Scotland and Wales, respectively.

Participants were followed from the date of their last valid dietary recall until the first occurrence of CAD, T2D or CKD, death, loss to follow-up or the end of outcome ascertainment based on the nation-specific censor dates, whichever came first.

To assess the generalizability of the factors, the H-matrix was frozen from the discovery dataset and held-out participants were projected onto it using non-negative least squares (NNLS) via scikit-learn's NMF.transform().

After participant exclusions, UKB participants recruited in England were randomly split (70/30) into discovery and replication datasets and participants recruited in Scotland and Wales formed a geographically independent validation dataset.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

live_data_statements: Participants had a mean age (SD) of 59.2 (7.8) years, mean body mass index (BMI) of 26.3 (4.3) kg/m 2 and 57.0% were female (Extended Data Table 1).
We applied NMF to the reported intake of 148 individual foods and beverages in a discovery dataset of 55,839 UKB participants recruited in England (70% random sample; Fig. 1b).

The remaining participants recruited in England formed a replication dataset (n = 23,932) and participants recruited in Scotland and Wales formed a geographically independent validation dataset (n = 7,391; Fig. 1a).

We tested each factor in relation to incident CAD, T2D and CKD using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic and lifestyle covariates in the combined sample of participants recruited in England (n = 79,771; Methods; Fig. 1c).
The UKB study received ethical approval from the NHS National Research Ethics Service (Ref 11/NW/0382), and all participants provided informed consent.

Participants were recruited from 2006 to 2010 at 22 assessment centers across England, Scotland and Wales, with baseline information, health and lifestyle questionnaires, physical measures and biological samples collected according to standardized procedures [45] [46] [47] .
Between 2009 and 2012 a subset of participants completed up to five online 24hour dietary recall assessments using the Oxford WebQ 48 .

The discovery (n=55,839) and replication (n=23,932) datasets included participants recruited from assessment centers in England using a 70/30 random split stratified by age, sex and number of valid dietary recalls.
The validation dataset (n=7,391) included all participants recruited from Scotland and Wales, providing an independent test of generalizability across regional dietary cultures.

First occurrences data were accessed on 22 September 2022, with censoring dates of 30 September 2021, 31 July 2021, and 31 October 2021 for participants recruited in England, Scotland and Wales, respectively.

Participants were followed from the date of their last valid dietary recall until the first occurrence of CAD, T2D or CKD, death, loss to follow-up or the end of outcome ascertainment based on the nation-specific censor dates, whichever came first.

To assess the generalizability of the factors, the H-matrix was frozen from the discovery dataset and held-out participants were projected onto it using non-negative least squares (NNLS) via scikit-learn's NMF.transform().

After participant exclusions, UKB participants recruited in England were randomly split (70/30) into discovery and replication datasets and participants recruited in Scotland and Wales formed a geographically independent validation dataset.
